q: What is the clearest intended source of hierarchy?
o: The entrance is dominant primarily because it has the greatest floor area.
The circular hall establishes a repeating structural rhythm throughout the complex.
The entrance is differentiated primarily by shape within a repeated context.
All galleries necessarily become equally prominent because their areas are similar.
n: Hierarchy can be established through shape as well as size or location. A distinct form may give the entrance a recognizable role among repeated rectangular elements even when their areas are comparable. Its effectiveness still depends on visibility and the surrounding arrangement. The scenario supplies no evidence that greater size is the cause of prominence.

q: Which study extends the design beyond changing the plan outline?
o: Rotate the plan symbol while keeping all roof and opening conditions unchanged.
Assume a fan-shaped plan guarantees even illumination at every reading position.
Evaluate lighting from the plan outline before studying roof and opening geometry.
Test roof and clerestory geometry in section against daylight and spatial requirements.
n: The library discussion shows that transformation occurs in section as well as plan. Roof profiles and high-level openings influence how daylight enters and how a hall is experienced. A plan shape cannot establish lighting performance by itself. The appropriate next step is to study the three-dimensional relationship and test the proposed light distribution.

s: A shared reference versus mere proximity
q: What must be established before calling the hall an effective datum for those objects?
o: A requirement that every object be arranged in four radial sectors.
A discernible organizing relationship between the containing space and the elements.
A rule that each object must have identical material and dimensions.
Only the fact that all objects are physically inside the same building.
n: A containing volume can act as a datum, but co-location alone does not explain an organizing relationship. The lecture emphasizes a shared reference through which diverse parts are understood. The designer should be able to identify that relationship in the arrangement instead of applying the label simply because an enclosure exists.

q: What programme response best follows the lecture’s transformation case?
o: Add all new uses to any available leftover area without checking their relationships.
Treat the original activity list as permanently complete because the building is still called a library.
Remove quiet study automatically because newer activities have appeared.
Reassess the activity mix and relationships while maintaining the institution’s core purpose.
ref: Zoom lecture 05:53:00–06:02:00; JKMM Architects — Seinäjoki City Library: https://jkmm.fi/work/seinajoki-library/
n: The library case treats the programme as responsive to changing ways of accessing and sharing knowledge. New social or digital activities need consideration alongside retained quiet uses. Revisiting the programme does not require abandoning the institution’s purpose; it identifies how that purpose can be supported through a different mix of spaces.

q: Which evaluation best addresses transformation?
o: Judge the addition only by whether its materials copy the older façade.
Accept every change solely because both buildings are called libraries.
Reject transformation because all external silhouettes must remain unchanged.
Examine what remains recognizable and how the changes respond to new requirements.
n: Transformation combines change with an intelligible continuity. The lecture uses a library to show that changing forms and activities can respond to a developing programme. The name alone does not establish successful continuity, and identical appearance is not the only means of preserving it. Evaluate purpose, spatial relationships, context and what the scheme deliberately retains.

q: Which statement is justified?
o: The elevation proves every internal space has a matching counterpart.
A symmetrical elevation requires radial organization of the whole site.
The interior differences make it impossible for the elevation to be symmetrical.
The elevation can be symmetrical without establishing symmetry throughout the plan.
n: Symmetry must be assessed within a stated view or arrangement. Correspondence in the elevation does not prove that all internal functions, rooms or services mirror across the building. The lecture’s qualification of precedent readings helps avoid extending a visible relationship beyond the evidence being examined.

q: Which conclusion is supported by this arrangement?
o: The unequal room sizes prevent the path from organizing the composition.
The path is an axis only when every room entrance lies on its centreline.
The common path makes the rooms bilaterally symmetrical despite their differences.
The path can establish an axis without producing bilateral symmetry.
n: An axis provides a line of organization; symmetry requires corresponding arrangements about an axis or centre. The same layout can therefore be axial and asymmetrical. Keeping these concepts distinct allows a designer to preserve a strong route while accommodating different room requirements. A shared organizing line does not erase differences between the parts.

q: Which reading avoids an overly restrictive interpretation of hierarchy?
o: Hierarchy applies only between separate buildings and cannot describe this plan.
The surrounding rooms eliminate hierarchy because they share the same roof.
The hall can have hierarchy only if its exterior is a different colour.
The hall can establish internal hierarchy through its size and spatial position.
n: The lecture later extends hierarchy to internal spaces, despite an earlier restrictive remark about a single building. A hall can become an organizing focus through its dimensions, position or distinctive shape. Hierarchy is a relationship among parts and is not limited to a collection of detached buildings. An exterior colour change is not a prerequisite.

q: Which design issue should guide evaluation of that connection?
o: Continuity of use and circulation together with the distinct identities of both parts.
Whether the new programme can avoid any relationship with the existing collections.
Whether the connection makes the two buildings visually identical from every approach.
Whether underground placement automatically removes all accessibility requirements.
ref: Zoom lecture 05:53:00–06:02:00; Alvar Aalto Foundation — Aalto Library in Seinäjoki: https://visit.alvaraalto.fi/en/destinations/seinajoki-library/; JKMM Architects — Seinäjoki City Library: https://jkmm.fi/work/seinajoki-library/
n: The Seinäjoki example links old and new while allowing a new architectural expression and expanded public role. A connection must be evaluated as a usable route, not merely a line on a diagram. Its below-ground location does not establish accessibility or wayfinding quality. Preservation and adaptation can be addressed together through carefully considered spatial relationships.

q: What should the designer check before claiming effective supervision?
o: Whether the roof silhouette can be used as sufficient evidence of interior visibility.
Whether shelving and internal obstructions preserve the intended sightlines.
Whether the fan outline can be drawn without any rectilinear support rooms.
Whether equal floor areas can substitute for checking views from the service point.
ref: Zoom lecture 05:46:00–05:52:00; Alvar Aalto Foundation — Aalto Library in Seinäjoki: https://visit.alvaraalto.fi/en/destinations/seinajoki-library/
n: The fan arrangement can make several areas visible from a common service position, but the outline alone does not guarantee supervision. Shelving, partitions and level changes can obstruct views. Aalto’s library combines a fan-shaped hall with rectilinear support functions; the functional relationship matters more than making every component conform to one geometry.

q: Why might the first pavilion read as more important?
o: Its identical dimensions necessarily prevent any difference in perceived importance.
Its hierarchy proves that its interior contains a more important programme.
Its approach position and visual exposure distinguish it from the other pavilion.
The difference is best explained by size hierarchy, despite their equal dimensions.
n: Location and foreground can establish prominence without a larger building. The main approach makes one pavilion a visual destination and leaves space for it to be perceived. This is a compositional reading, not evidence of structural strength or the actual importance of its programme. Hierarchy should be considered from the intended sequence of arrival.

s: Quiet and active uses in an expanded library
q: What does this reveal about a split programme?
o: The presence of social activity proves that quiet reading should be removed.
A connecting passage makes it unnecessary to consider the intended character of each area.
Separation into different parts still requires careful design of their connection and interaction.
Different building volumes guarantee that activities cannot interfere.
n: The lecture presents separating active and quieter uses as one strategy within the library expansion. Its effectiveness depends on how the parts connect and function, not simply on assigning them to different buildings. The link should support continuity while respecting the distinct requirements that motivated the split programme.

q: Which interpretation distinguishes the arrangements?
o: A demonstrates bilateral correspondence; B demonstrates radial organization.
A demonstrates radial organization; B demonstrates bilateral correspondence only.
Both require a single linear entrance-to-exit route to establish their symmetry.
Neither has symmetry because the rooms are separated by circulation space.
n: Bilateral symmetry relates corresponding parts across a line or plane. Radial symmetry organizes equivalent elements around a centre. These descriptions refer to the arrangement shown, not a guarantee of how an entire real building works. The figure deliberately isolates the two relationships so that circulation or site differences do not have to be guessed.

q: How should the number of sectors affect its classification?
o: Eight sectors establish only bilateral symmetry and exclude radial organization.
It can have radial symmetry; the principle does not require exactly four sectors.
It cannot have radial symmetry because the lecture’s teaching axes form four quadrants.
The repeated sectors become a linear sequence simply because there are more than four.
n: Radial organization relates repeated parts to a centre. Four quadrants may help explain the idea, but they are not a required number of sectors. The diagram’s actual correspondence should determine the analysis rather than converting one explanatory sketch into a universal rule for all radial arrangements.

q: How does the terrace help organize the precinct?
o: It establishes a common plane against which the separate buildings are understood.
It ensures all building roofs occupy an identical horizontal plane.
It produces bilateral symmetry regardless of the buildings’ positions.
It gives every building the same internal structural system.
n: A common platform can function as a planar datum. It provides continuity at the base of elements that differ above it. The relationship does not require equal roof heights, identical construction or symmetrical positions. The lecture’s datum examples show how unity can arise from a reference shared by diverse parts.

q: What additional evidence is needed before calling the plan a rhythm of repeated rooms?
o: A central axis that mirrors the building’s external outline.
A uniform exterior paint specification across every repeated panel.
A recurring spatial unit or interval in the plan, rather than façade repetition alone.
An entrance located at the midpoint of the external elevation.
n: A repetitive façade can create a visual rhythm without a corresponding rhythm of internal rooms. The later lecture examples concern repeated bays and spatial modules. Establishing that claim requires evidence in the plan or section, such as recurring units and intervals. A central entrance or symmetrical outline is not required for repetition.

q: What should be concluded about the plan’s rhythm?
o: The balconies alone establish that all internal dwellings have different programmes.
Spatial rhythm can be identified only from a completely uniform façade.
The repeated spatial rhythm can remain even when the exterior articulation varies.
Any exterior variation proves that the dwelling modules cannot repeat internally.
n: The lecture distinguishes actual repeated spaces from their external representation. Variations in balcony treatment or façade articulation do not necessarily eliminate a recurring dwelling module. Reading both plan and elevation avoids inferring the internal arrangement from appearance alone and allows the designer to consider how the two expressions relate.

s: Transferring a sightline principle between typologies
q: Which lesson can transfer without copying the library’s fan outline?
o: Treat supervision as a façade issue because shelves are movable furniture.
Convert the shop into a fan regardless of its site and customer route.
Arrange the observation point and obstructions so that the required areas can actually be seen.
Assume a centrally named checkout can see every aisle without a plan study.
n: The lecture itself compares library supervision with convenience-store checkout sightlines. The transferable relationship is between a real observation point and the areas that need visibility. Copying the outline is unnecessary: furniture, partitions and aisles should be tested from the staffed position within the requirements of the new typology.

s: Addition and subtraction as design operations
q: What should the transformation be evaluated against?
o: The purposes of the changes and the defining relationships retained or altered by them.
The exterior outline alone, without considering the new spaces or activities.
The assumption that keeping one route makes every other change successful.
The assumption that any addition automatically destroys the scheme’s identity.
n: Addition and subtraction can change a form while preserving an intelligible relationship to its earlier organization. The lecture treats transformation as disciplined exploration, so each operation needs a purpose and evaluation. Continuity is neither automatic nor impossible: it depends on what the project defines as important and how the altered scheme works.

s: Accommodating change while retaining existing fabric
q: Why might the addition be a useful design option?
o: It can accommodate new requirements while reducing pressure to force them into the old interior.
Keeping the old exterior alone establishes that all significant spatial character is preserved.
A new building makes the relationship to the existing library irrelevant.
Any addition automatically resolves every heritage and contextual concern.
ref: Zoom lecture 05:53:00–06:02:00; Alvar Aalto Foundation — Aalto Library in Seinäjoki: https://visit.alvaraalto.fi/en/destinations/seinajoki-library/; JKMM Architects — Seinäjoki City Library: https://jkmm.fi/work/seinajoki-library/
n: The lecture interprets the connected library addition as a way to keep the older building active while accommodating new demands elsewhere. This is an option to evaluate, not an automatic conservation approval. Its value depends on both the significant existing relationships and the quality of the connection, programme and new work.

q: What is the walkway’s principal ordering role?
o: It removes the need to consider how each pavilion is reached.
It provides a shared linear reference that relates the different elements.
It establishes radial symmetry around each individual pavilion.
It makes the different pavilions geometrically identical.
n: A linear datum can connect and relate dissimilar elements without making them identical. The common walkway gives the collection a readable relationship and can also carry circulation. Its presence does not automatically resolve every access issue. The ordering principle concerns the shared reference, while usability must still be checked.

q: Which datum is most directly being used?
o: An identical room module that makes all surrounding rooms the same size.
A radial symmetry that must exist whenever rooms face an atrium.
A volumetric datum, established by the shared organizing space.
A planar datum established solely by a line drawn on one wall.
n: A courtyard or atrium can serve as a volumetric datum when surrounding elements relate to it as a shared spatial reference. The role depends on the arrangement, not simply on the atrium being large or empty. Unlike rooms can remain distinct while the common volume helps make their relationships legible.

q: Which response best combines rhythm with a meaningful exception?
o: Keep repetition only on the façade and disregard the relationship to internal spaces.
Retain the repeated dwelling system while making the lounge a deliberate variation.
Change every dwelling bay to prevent the shared lounge from appearing different.
Force the lounge into an unchanged dwelling plan even if its activities no longer fit.
n: Rhythm may organize repeated spatial units, while hierarchy can distinguish a shared or special space. A meaningful exception need not destroy the organizing system. The lecture connects repetition to programme rather than requiring every room to be identical. Forcing a different use into an unsuitable module prioritizes pattern over function.

s: One overhead plane relating varied parts
q: How can that roof contribute to order?
o: It establishes a central axis regardless of how the booths are arranged.
It can act as a planar datum relating otherwise varied components.
It makes all booths equivalent in programme and dimensions.
It prevents any component beneath it from having its own hierarchy.
n: The lecture uses varied convention booths under a shared roof to explain a planar datum. The overhead plane provides continuity while the subordinate parts can differ. A common reference does not force identical functions or eliminate other principles; hierarchy and circulation still need to be designed within the shared enclosure.

s: A prototype as a starting point
q: How should the prototype be used?
o: As a silhouette to copy even when its programme assumptions do not fit.
As a mandatory final template that all libraries must follow.
As evidence that alternatives no longer require comparison.
As a starting structure that can be transformed while its useful relationships are evaluated.
n: The lecture’s hypothetical linear library illustrates transformation rather than a universal typological rule. A prototype makes relationships available for testing and alteration. Its value is retained where it supports the requirements; the designer should not preserve its geometry simply because it appeared first or came from a precedent.

q: What is the likely compositional problem?
o: Making all parts equally prominent necessarily creates a clear hierarchy.
Distinctive components eliminate the need to consider a user’s route.
Hierarchy requires that every room have exactly the same function.
Competing emphasis has weakened the ranking that should distinguish the principal destination.
n: Hierarchy depends on relative importance, so equal or competing prominence can make the intended ranking difficult to perceive. The lecture warns against making every part a focal event. Differentiation should help users understand the arrangement and find important destinations, rather than producing an undirected collection of attention-seeking components.

q: What is the most defensible correction?
o: Accept the rejection because a datum must extend infinitely in physical space.
Assess its organizing relationship; endpoints alone do not disqualify a datum.
Rename it a plane because every finite organizing element must be planar.
Remove its endpoints so that the plan can have an organizing reference.
n: The lecture contrasts axis and datum using endpoints, but that distinction is too absolute. A datum is understood through its reference role and may be physically bounded. An axis and a linear datum can overlap in a composition. The useful question is how elements relate to the line, not whether the drawing gives it ends.

q: What relationship needs reconsideration?
o: The assumption that hierarchy can relate to an internal activity.
The connection between the visually prominent form and the programme’s intended principal space.
The idea that an exterior form can ever communicate spatial importance.
The requirement that every service store have a different construction system.
n: The Florence and Chandigarh examples connect major form to significant internal space. A mismatch can undermine the intended reading when the strongest architectural expression marks a secondary function. This does not mean every room must be literally displayed outside, but the proposed hierarchy should support the stated organizing purpose.

q: What is the strongest reason not to force both parts into the same geometry?
o: Different activities and relationships can justify different forms within a coordinated whole.
Support rooms have no relationship to the library’s overall operation.
Using two geometries removes the need to coordinate their junction or circulation.
A fan-shaped reading area requires every other room to become radial.
ref: Zoom lecture 05:46:00–05:52:00; Alvar Aalto Foundation — Aalto Library in Seinäjoki: https://visit.alvaraalto.fi/en/destinations/seinajoki-library/
n: The Seinäjoki discussion combines regular support accommodation with a fan-shaped public hall. The relationship illustrates functional differentiation within one institution. Coherence does not demand one shape for every activity, but the parts still need workable connections and a shared design intent rather than remaining unrelated fragments.
